CHAPTER I 
INTRODUCTION 
Safe driving depends not only on road conditions, traffic regulations, and vehicle 
performance but also on the driver’s ability to remain alert while operating a vehicle. Driver 
drowsiness is a serious road-safety concern because reduced alertness can impair attention, reaction 
time, judgment, and decision -making while driving. In the Philippine setting, the Land 
Transportation Office, as reported by the Philippine Information Agency, emphasized that drivers 
should pull over and rest when they feel tired. S imilarly, Fonseca and Ferreira identified driver 
drowsiness as a significant road -safety issue associated with impaired attentional control, slower 
reaction time, reduced decision-making ability, and an increased risk of crashes and severe injuries 
(Philippine Information Agency, 2025; Fonseca & Ferreira, 2025). When drivers continue operating 
a vehicle despite visible signs of drowsiness, their ability to maintain the sustained attention 
required for safe driving may become compromised. 
In the Philippines, road traffic crashes remain a major public -safety issue. The World 
Health Organization Philippines and the Department of Transportation reported that road traffic 
deaths in the country increased by 39%, from 7,938 deaths in 2011 to 11,0 96 deaths in 2021. The 
same source reported that road traffic injuries are the leading cause of death among Filipinos aged 
15 to 29 years old and cost approximately 2.6% of the country’s gross domestic product. In response 
to this concern, the Philippine Road Safety Action Plan 2023–2028 was launched as the country’s 
blueprint for road-safety initiatives, with the goal of reducing road traffic deaths by 35% by 2028 
(World Health Organization Philippines & Department of Transportation, 2023). The Philippine 
Statistics Authority also reported that deaths due to land transport accidents reached 13,125 in 2023, 
accounting for 1.9% of all deaths in the country. Meanwhile, the Asian Transport Observatory 
reported that road crashes and serious injuries cost the Phi lippines approximately USD 11 billion 
in 2021, equivalent to about 3% of the country’s gross domestic product (Philippine Statistics 
Authority, 2025; Asian Transport Observatory, 2025). Although Philippine statistics do not 
separately identify the number of crashes associated with driver drowsiness, Reyes (2025) reported 
that international estimates attribute up to 30% of road accidents to driver fatigue. The same report 
explained that sleepiness associated with drowsy driving slows reaction time, decreases awareness, 
impairs judgment, and increases the risk of crashes. These conditions demonstrate the need for 
preventive and technology-supported road-safety systems that can assist drivers before dangerous 
situations become more serious. 
Human behavior and driver condition are also important considerations in road safety. 
Segun et al. (2024) identified human behavior, public awareness, infrastructure, technological

interventions, and enforcement as factors associated with road -crash incidents in Metro Manila. 
Road safety therefore involves not only road and vehicle conditions but also the driver’s physical 
and mental condition. Because drowsiness may reduce alertness and responsiveness, technologies 
that monitor visible signs of drowsiness may help drivers recognize possible declines in 
attentiveness while driving. 
Emerging technologies in intelligent transportation provide new methods for detecting 
possible driver drowsiness before it develops into a more serious safety risk. Computer vision and 
artificial intelligence have been widely explored in driver -drowsiness detection systems because 
they can analyze visible indicators such as eye closure, yawning, mouth movement, and changes in 
head posture. Albadawi et al. (2022) explained that advances in computing technology and artificial 
intelligence have contributed to the development of more capable driver -drowsiness detection 
systems. However, the practical implementation of these systems may still be affected by lighting 
conditions, device capability, detection reliability, and system accessibility. These limitations 
highlight the need for a driver -monitoring system designed to operate under practical in -vehicle 
conditions. 
The background of this study is grounded in the integration of computer vision, artificial 
intelligence, the Internet of Things, and mobile -based driver monitoring. Camera -based systems 
can observe selected visible signs of drowsiness without requiring wea rable sensors or direct 
vehicle integration. Lighting conditions remain an important consideration because camera -based 
facial measurements depend on usable image quality. DriveAlert uses an infrared-capable camera, 
and its performance under different available -light conditions will be evaluated usin g the final 
hardware configuration . Local processing is also important because warning systems should 
respond promptly even when internet access or mobile data is unavailable. Edge and localized 
processing can reduce latency and support privacy-sensitive Internet of Things applications, while 
ESP32 documentation supports Wi-Fi capability and local communication between the IoT device 
and the smartphone (Andriulo et al., 2024; Espressif Systems, 2025; Espressif Systems, 2026). 
When combined with Android-based processing and local offline Wi -Fi communication, these 
technologies can support a more accessible driver-drowsiness monitoring system. 
This study proposes DriveAlert, an Internet of Things-based driver drowsiness monitoring 
and alert system that uses computer vision and artificial intelligence. The system is designed to 
monitor selected visible signs of drowsiness, specifically prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head 
nodding. When a selected behavior satisfies its established duration, repetition, or temporal -
confirmation condition, DriveAlert activates a warning alert. Thres hold-based alerting is 
appropriate because driver-drowsiness detection systems should not rely on a single uncertain video

3 
 
frame and should instead evaluate whether a visible behavior is sustained or repeated before 
activating a warning (Albadawi et al., 2023; Essel et al., 2025). DriveAlert also stores distinct 
confirmed warning events for Driver review and applies staged intervention when qualifying 
warning activity recurs or persists. Warning Stage 1 provides the initial selected warning sound, 
and Warning Stage 2 retains that sound as an intermediate warning state. Warning Stage 3 combines 
the selected sound with a prerecorded spoken rest advisory and introduces Trusted Contact

not represent medical or physiological drowsiness severity. 
Rationale of the Study 
Driver drowsiness may not always be recognized immediately while a person is operating 
a vehicle. Although drivers may stop and rest once they become aware that they are sleepy, 
observable changes associated with reduced alertness may appear before they re spond to their 
condition. Rajkumarsingh and Totah (2021) explained that drowsiness can affect judgment and 
decision-making, while Ayas et al. (2024) found that driver -state monitoring systems commonly 
combine detection with warning interventions. This creates a need for a supplementary system that 
can monitor selected visible signs of drowsiness and provide a timely warning without replacing 
the driver’s responsibility to stop and rest. 
Visible changes involving the eyes, mouth, and head are commonly examined in driver -
drowsiness monitoring because they can be observed without attaching physiological sensors to the 
driver. Rajkumarsingh and Totah (2021) considered blinking duration, yawni ng frequency, and 
head position, while Albadawi et al. (2023) examined eye condition, mouth opening, and head pose 
as visual features associated with drowsiness. These findings are relevant to the selected indicators 
monitored by DriveAlert: prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding. Monitoring these 
behaviors provides a non-contact method of identifying observable changes that may be associated 
with reduced alertness. 
However, ordinary driver behavior may resemble a visible sign of drowsiness. Brief eye 
closure may represent normal blinking, mouth opening may occur while speaking, and downward 
head movement may result from briefly looking at another area inside the vehi cle. Responding to 
every isolated movement may therefore produce unnecessary warnings. Albadawi et al. (2023) 
evaluated visual indicators across a temporal window, while Quiles -Cucarella et al. (2024) and 
Essel et al. (2025) applied time-based or consecutive-frame conditions before activating warnings. 
These approaches demonstrate the importance of confirming that a behavior is sustained or repeated 
rather than relying on a single uncertain observation.

4 
 
Warning reliability is also important because detection has limited value when the resulting 
alert is unclear, easily ignored, or repeatedly activated by incorrect detections. Ayas et al. (2024) 
found that driver-drowsiness mitigation systems commonly use auditory warnings and may apply 
different levels of intervention. Weibull et al. (2024) also showed that false alarms can influence 
how drivers respond to later warnings. A drowsiness -warning system must therefore balance 
responsiveness and consistency so that the driver is alerted when the established detection 
conditions are satisfied without producing excessive interruptions during ordinary movements. 
DriveAlert applies three Warning Stages to manage recurrent or persistent qualifying 
warning activity. The first distinct confirmed warning event occurring while no Warning Stage is 
active immediately activates Stage 1 and begins a 60-second evaluation period. If another distinct 
confirmed warning event occurs while Stage 1 is active, the system immediately progresses to Stage 
2 and begins a new 60 -second evaluation period. A subsequent distinct confirmed warning event 
during Stage 2 immediately activates S tage 3. When no new distinct event occurs, the system 
evaluates whether a qualifying behavior remains persistently active at the 60 -second boundary. 
Persistent qualifying activity causes progression from Stage 1 to Stage 2 or from Stage 2 to Stage 
3. If no qualifying behavior remains active, Stage 1 returns to the normal state, while Stage 2 de -
escalates to Stage 1. Stage 3 is the maximum intervention level. Recurrent events during Stage 3 
may reactivate its warning without restarting the current evaluation period. At the Stage 3 boundary, 
recurrent or persistent qualifying activity maintains Stage 3; otherwise, the system de-escalates to 
Stage 2. Stages 1 and 2 use the selected warning sound, while Stage 3 adds a spoken rest advisory 
and Trusted Contact synchronization eligibility. These stages describe system intervention rather 
than medical or physiological drowsiness severity. 
An immediate warning addresses a detected condition at a particular moment, but the 
warning alone provides little information after it has ended. Without an organized record, the driver 
may be unable to review when an alert occurred, which visible sign was detected, or whether alerts 
appeared repeatedly during a monitoring session. Hidayat and Ibnugraha (2025) developed a 
system described as a driver-fatigue monitoring system that displayed detection results through a 
web-based dashboard, while Kashyap et a l. (2025) stored driver -status information, detection 
timestamps, and historical records for later review. These studies show that recorded events can 
remain useful beyond the immediate warning by providing structured information for later review. 
Stored drowsiness-alert events may also be summarized to make the recorded information 
easier to interpret. Retained alerts may be organized into alert counts, detected-sign summaries, the 
highest Warning Stage associated with their stored warning events, alert trends, and Stage 3 
synchronization status. Monitoring-session summaries separately identify the highest intervention

5 
 
stage reached during each session. These summaries allow users to review patterns in the available 
records without examining every alert individually. Their purpose is descriptive and should not be 
interpreted as medical analysis, accident prediction, confirmation of drowsiness, or proof that a 
driver is safe or unsafe to continue driving. 
Drowsiness-alert records may also support secondary awareness through an approved 
Trusted Contact. DriveAlert stores all distinct confirmed warning events for Driver review but 
limits external synchronization according to its Warning Stage 3 rule. When DriveAlert first enters 
Warning Stage 3, one Stage 3 transition record becomes eligible for Trusted Contact 
synchronization. Individual confirmed warning events occurring during the active Stage 3 period 
remain in the Driver’s alert history and do not each independently create synchronization records. 
When a 60-second Stage 3 evaluation period ends, DriveAlert creates one synchronization-eligible 
persistence update if at least one additional distinct confirmed warning event occurred during that 
period or a qualifying behavior remains persistently active  at its boundary. Either condition 
maintains Stage 3 and begins another 60-second evaluation period. If neither condition is present, 
the system de-escalates to Stage 2 without creating a persistence update for the completed period. 
The reviewed approaches provide visible-sign monitoring, warning delivery, event storage, 
dashboard viewing, physical alarm output, offline operation, and authorized record access in 
different combinations. Some systems concentrate mainly on detecting a visible sign and producing 
an immediate warning, while others emphasize historical records, dashboards, or remote 
monitoring. The need addressed by this study is therefore not the absence of driver -drowsiness 
technology but the opportunity to combine selecte d functions that support the driver during 
monitoring and preserve relevant information after a warning has been issued. 
DriveAlert addresses these connected needs by monitoring prolonged eye closure, 
yawning, and head nodding and providing an audio warning when a selected behavior satisfies its 
established detection condition. It also stores distinct confirmed alert episodes locally, presents 
descriptive summaries of retained records for Driver review, and synchronizes only eligible Stage 
3 transition records and Stage 3 persistence updates for access by an approved Trusted Cont act 
when internet connectivity becomes available. Through this integration, DriveAlert connects 
visible-sign monitoring, warning delivery, event recording, record review, and authorized 
information sharing within one driver -focused system. It is intended as a supplementary driver -
support tool and does not  medically or physiologically confirm drowsiness, determine whether a 
driver is fit to continue driving, replace adequate rest, or control the vehicle.

Objectives of the Study 
This study aims to develop DriveAlert, an Internet of Things -based system designed to assist 
drivers by monitoring selected visible signs of drowsiness, providing warning alerts, storing 
drowsiness-alert records, and synchronizing these records with a connected Trusted Contact when 
internet connectivity becomes available. 
Specifically, this study pursues the following objectives:  
1. To gather data on the occurrence of drowsiness and observable signs associated with it 
among drivers while driving. 
2. To design and implement a computer-vision algorithm capable of detecting prolonged 
eye closure, yawning, and head nodding using driver-specific detection thresholds and 
temporal-confirmation conditions for triggering warning alerts. 
3. To design and implement a local Wi -Fi communication architecture between the IoT 
device and the driver’s smartphone that enables real -time drowsiness -sign monitoring 
without requiring internet or mobile data connectivity. 
4. To implement an alarm system in which the IoT device receives wireless warning 
commands from the smartphone and produces predefined audio warning alerts through an 
onboard speaker. 
5. To develop a dashboard that records and displays drowsiness-alert events and synchronizes 
drowsiness-alert records with a connected Trusted Contact when internet connectivity 
becomes available. 
Scope and Limitations 
This study focuses on the development and pilot evaluation of DriveAlert, an IoT -based 
driver drowsiness monitoring and alert system using computer vision. The system monitors 
prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding through an IoT device equipped with an 
infrared-capable camera and an onboard speaker. Dedicated infrared LEDs and external infrared 
illuminators are excluded from the final prototype. 
An Android mobile application processes the captured video locally using calibrated EAR 
and MAR thresholds, a fixed 15° downward head-pitch deviation relative to the Driver’s calibrated 
neutral position, and sign-specific temporal-confirmation conditions. After a selected visible sign 
satisfies its complete confirmation condition, DriveAlert creates a confirmed warning event, applies 
the appropriate Warning Stage, requests the corresponding warning output, and stores the event 
locally for Driver review. Sep arate Stage 3 transition records and qualifying Stage 3 persistence 
updates become eligible for synchronization with an approved Trusted Contact when internet 
connectivity becomes available.

7 
 
DriveAlert is intended for drivers of four -wheeled and larger vehicles. Motorcycles and 
other two -wheeled vehicles are excluded because of differences in driver position, camera 
placement, weather exposure, and operating conditions. The system will be eval uated only under 
controlled or simulated driving conditions and will not be tested for long -term use during actual 
road travel, heavy traffic, severe weather, uneven roads, or other unpredictable conditions. 
DriveAlert is limited to monitoring three selected visible signs associated with drowsiness: 
prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding. The system does not medically or 
physiologically confirm that a driver is drowsy. These behaviors may occur for r easons unrelated 
to drowsiness, while a drowsy driver may not always display them clearly. The system may 
therefore generate false alerts or miss relevant events. It does not detect sleep disorders, stress, 
illness, medication effects, alcohol influence, or other causes of reduced alertness, and it does not 
use physiological or wearable sensors. 
Detection performance may be affected by camera placement, Driver position, head 
orientation, facial obstruction, eyeglasses, sunglasses, masks, glare, lighting conditions, sudden 
movement, reflections, and image quality. Although dedicated infrared illumination was included 
in the initial design, it was excluded from the final prototype due to limitations encountered during 
hardware development. The available infrared LED configuration did not provide sufficient facial 
illumination at the intended camera -to-Driver distance. Attempts to improve illumination by 
increasing the number of infrared LEDs also resulted in unstable operation of the breadboard power 
supply setup, including intermittent power loss and interruptions affecting connected components. 
These issues prevented the expanded LED configuration from operating reliably and limited further 
improvements to infrared illumination using the available hardware. These limitations apply 
specifically to the configuration tested in this study and do not esta blish that infrared illumination 
is unsuitable for driver monitoring in general. The final prototype therefore depends on available 
light, and its infrared-capable camera does not guarantee reliable assessment under extremely low-
light or no-light conditions. DriveAlert pauses drowsiness-sign assessment when facial lighting is 
insufficient, even if a face remains detected. Assessment also pauses when reliable facial tracking 
is unavailable or fewer than two monitored signs remain available. Frames rejected because of 
insufficient lighting do not advance calibration’s required valid measurement time. Assessment 
resumes when the applicable visibility, lighting-quality, and observation-freshness requirements are 
restored. These assessment pauses do not by themselves end the monitoring session.  DriveAlert 
also provides operational guidance that is separate from drowsiness-stage warnings. During eligible 
active monitoring, sustained inactivity may produce a “No movement detected” status after ten 
seconds and a spoken movement advisory after twenty-five seconds. These timings are provisional

The system does not automatically identify individual drivers. In shared vehicles, each

System performance may depend on the Android smartphone’s processing power, memory,

Significance of the Study 
The study brings benefits to various stakeholders involved in or affected by the 
development and implementation of DriveAlert. 
Drivers. Drivers are the primary beneficiaries of DriveAlert. They may benefit from real-
time monitoring of selected visible signs of drowsiness, predefined audio warning alerts with 
adjustable volume and an enforced minimum level, and a dashboard that records an d summarizes 
drowsiness-alert events. Through the dashboard, Drivers can review alert counts, detected -sign

summaries, the highest Warning Stage associated with their stored warning events, alert trends, and 
Stage 3 synchronization status. Session summaries separately identify the highest intervention stage 
reached during an individual monitoring session. 
Trusted Contacts. Trusted Contacts may benefit from accessing synchronization-eligible 
Stage 3 transition records and Stage 3 persistence updates when internet connectivity becomes 
available. These records provide secondary awareness when qualifying warning activity reaches or 
continues at DriveAlert’s maximum intervention stage. The feature supports synchronized record 
review and does not function as live Driver monitoring or an emergency-response service. 
Passengers. Passengers may indirectly benefit from DriveAlert because the system 
provides a warning when a selected visible sign of drowsiness satisfies its established detection 
condition. The warning may prompt the driver to reassess their condition and take appro priate 
action, such as stopping and resting. 
Researchers. The researchers will gain practical experience in Internet of Things

Theoretical Background 
This study is anchored primarily in Vigilance Theory, which explains how sustained 
attention and alertness may decline during prolonged monitoring tasks. Mackworth (1948) 
introduced the concept of vigilance decrement through research showing that a person’s ability to 
detect important signals may decrease over time. In driving, this theory is relevant because drivers 
must maintain attention for extended periods, particularly during nighttime travel, long -distance 
driving, and monotonous road conditions. McW illiams and Ward (2021) explained that low -
demand and monotonous driving conditions may place drivers in a state of cognitive underload, 
contributing to vigilance decrement and reduced responsiveness to safety -critical events. For 
DriveAlert, Vigilance The ory provides a conceptual basis for understanding why maintaining 
alertness is important during prolonged or monotonous driving. The system itself is limited to 
monitoring prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding as selected visible signs associated 
with drowsiness. 
The study is further guided by Human Factors Engineering and Human -Centered Design 
principles. Human factors focus on designing systems according to human capabilities, limitations, 
behaviors, and possible errors. The Federal Highway Administration (n.d.) explained that human 
factors address the relationship between people and the systems they use, with consideration for 
human abilities and limitations. This is relevant to driver monitoring because warnings should be 
clear, timely, noticeable, and understandable without requiring complex interaction from the driver. 
Ayas et al. (2024) found that driver -drowsiness mitigation systems commonly use auditory 
warnings and may employ multistage interventions. These principles support DriveAlert’s use of 
predefined audio warnings, warning escalation, clear monitoring status, and an interface designed

to minimize driver interaction during active monitoring while allowing drowsiness-alert records to 
be reviewed afterward. 
Together, Vigilance Theory and human-centered design principles provide the theoretical 
and design foundation of DriveAlert. Vigilance Theory explains the importance of maintaining 
sustained attention during prolonged or monotonous driving, while Human Fac tors Engineering 
and Human-Centered Design guide how the system should communicate warnings and present 
information according to human capabilities and limitations. These foundations support 
DriveAlert’s development as a driver -centered drowsiness monitoring and alert system that 
combines visible -sign monitoring, warning output, drowsiness -alert record review, basic 
drowsiness insights, and Trusted Contact synchronization. 
Related Literature 
Driver sleepiness, sleep deprivation, and prolonged working hours are associated with 
increased road -traffic risk. Saleem (2022) identified sleepiness and sleep deprivation as 
contributors to road traffic accidents, while the National Highway Traffic Safet y Administration 
(n.d.) documented crashes and fatalities involving drowsy drivers. In the Philippine setting, Lu 
(2022) reported that prolonged working hours among bus and truck drivers may contribute to 
fatigue and sleepiness, thereby increasing road-accident risk. Segun et al. (2024) further identified 
human behavior and technology-supported interventions among the factors relevant to road safety. 
Together, these studies establish driver drowsiness as a road -safety concern and support the 
development of systems that monitor Driver behavior and provide timely warnings. 
Driver fatigue and drowsiness are related but distinct concepts. Fatigue broadly refers to 
mental or physical exhaustion, whereas drowsiness describes a sleep-like reduction in alertness that 
may precede sleep onset. Although some literature uses fatigue as a broader term when discussing 
reduced alertness, DriveAlert is specifically limited to selected visible signs associated with 
drowsiness and does not claim to detect fatigue as a whole. Hassan et al. (2026) identified prolonged 
or slow eyelid closure, y awning, and head nodding as behavioral manifestations of drowsiness. 
Albadawi et al. (2022) and Jan et al. (202 3) likewise identified eye closure, yawning, and head 
nodding among observable behaviors used in non -intrusive Driver-drowsiness detection. These 
findings support the selection of prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding as the three 
visible signs monitored by DriveAlert. 
Because these signs are externally observable, computer vision provides a non -invasive 
means of monitoring them without requiring physiological sensors. Albadawi et al. (2023) extracted 
Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR), Mouth Aspect Ratio (MAR), and head -pose featur es from facial 
landmarks using MediaPipe Face Mesh. Essel et al. (2025) similarly examined eye closure and

mouth aperture, while Kim et al. (2023) used infrared video and facial landmarks to evaluate eye 
closure and head orientation. These studies demonstrate that facial landmarks can support a 
common visual method for examining eye -, mouth-, and head -related behavior. However, facial 
measurements may still be affected by lighting, camera placement, face orientation, eyeglasses, 
facial obstruction, and individual facial characteristics. 
Eye Aspect Ratio represents the degree of eye openness using the relationship among 
selected eye landmarks and generally decreases as the upper and lower eyelids move closer 
together. Mouth Aspect Ratio similarly represents the degree of mouth opening and generally 
increases as the mouth opens wider (Albadawi et al., 2023). Head -pose estimation uses facial 
reference points to estimate changes in head orientation, while pitch represents upward or 
downward head rotation and may therefore support head-nodding analysis (Albadawi et al., 2023; 
Kim et al., 2023). Since ordinary blinking, speaking, and brief downward glances can temporarily 
produce similar measurements, a single threshold -crossing frame is insufficient to confirm a 
selected visible sign. 
Previous studies provide numerical values that can serve as initial references for 
DriveAlert, but these values should not automatically be applied to every Driver. Albadawi et al. 
(2023) selected an EAR threshold of 0.20 after evaluating different candida te values and eye 
characteristics. Higher values increased the possibility of normally open but smaller eyes being 
classified as closed, while lower values reduced the number of detected closed -eye frames. The 
same study selected a MAR threshold of 0.50 after considering differences in mouth characteristics; 
values that were too high could miss wide-mouth events among subjects with smaller mouths, while 
values that were too low increased the likelihood of ordinary talking or laughing being classified 
as mouth opening. These findings support 0.20 for EAR and 0.50 for MAR as literature-supported 
reference values rather than universal operational thresholds. 
Individual differences support the use of Driver -specific thresholds because fixed facial 
measurements may not generalize across users with different facial characteristics and normal head 
orientations. DriveAlert therefore uses four guided calibration phases, each requiring five seconds 
of valid measurements. During the neutral phase, the Driver faces forward with the eyes open to 
establish baseline EAR, MAR, and neutral head pitch. During the eyes -closed phase, closed-eye 
EAR is recorded as a calibration reference, although the operational EAR threshold remains 75% 
of the neutral open-eye baseline following Ersoy et al. (2026). During the mouth -open phase, the 
Driver keeps the mouth as open as possible, and the operational MAR threshold is set at 50% of 
the average open -mouth MAR following the personalized initialization approach of Quiles -
Cucarella et al. (2024), expressed as MARThreshold = OpenMouthMAR × 0.50. During the head-

approximately 12° to 20°, placing the selected 15° deviation within the reported range. These

approximately two seconds. Their system therefore used sustained eye closure exceeding two

Yawning requires a different duration because mouth opening associated with yawning is 
naturally a longer behavior. Dong et al. (2026) analyzed sustained mouth -opening duration and 
reported that separation between ordinary mouth movements and fatigue-related yawning became

exceeding three seconds as its yawning criterion. Quiles -Cucarella et al. (2024) likewise used a 
personalized MAR threshold together with a thre e-second mouth-opening condition. DriveAlert

before the required duration is completed, the temporal counter resets and no yawning event is

Head nodding requires a different confirmation approach because downward head

movement as an immediate warning condition.

maintaining the head away from the normal forward-facing position for a substantial portion of the 
observation period could still warrant warning. 
DriveAlert will therefore initially treat downward head rotation exceeding a fixed 15° 
deviation from the Driver’s calibrated neutral head position as a candidate head -nodding event

The three selected signs are therefore not given identical confirmation procedures because 
they present different sources of false detection. Sustained EAR measurements help distinguish 
prolonged eye closure from ordinary blinking, while sustained MAR meas urements help 
distinguish yawning from shorter mouth movements. Head movement is more ambiguous because 
normal Driver behavior can also involve downward pitch changes, making temporal persistence 
appropriate. DriveAlert consequently evaluates each selected  sign according to its own 
characteristics rather than requiring prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding to occur 
simultaneously. 
During uninterrupted valid observation, DriveAlert groups additional confirmed signs into 
the current alert episode while a previously active episode sign remains currently confirmed. These 
additional signs do not independently create another alert episode or advance the Warning Stage. A 
continuously confirmed sign does not repeatedly create distinct events merely because its 
measurement remains beyond its threshold. Its detector must be re-armed before the same sign can 
produce another confirmation. Tracking loss, stale observations, or assessment interruptions may 
break episode continuity; the system does not assume that a physical behavior remained 
continuously observable during an unavailable interval.

The 60-second value is not used as a confirmation threshold for prolonged eye closure, 
yawning, or head nodding. Those visible signs retain their independent Driver -specific 
measurement and temporal-confirmation conditions. Instead, 60 seconds represents t he warning-
stage evaluation interval used to determine whether persistent warning activity requires escalation 
or whether the absence of renewed qualifying activity permits de -escalation. A new distinct 
confirmed warning event may therefore cause earlier progression from Stage 1 to Stage 2 or from 
Stage 2 to Stage 3 without waiting for the corresponding 60 -second period to expire. Conversely, 
when no new distinct event occurs, the 60-second boundary provides a defined point for evaluating 
persistent activity or recovery. Schwarz et al. (2015) directly described progression when another 
drowsy episode occurred before mitigation abated or when the drowsy state persisted for 60 
seconds, while Gaspar et al. (2017) experimentally evaluated three-stage warnings using 60-second 
countermeasure states.  
Because Schwarz et al. (2015) and Gaspar et al. (2017) used a Driver -state algorithm that 
classified the Driver as awake or drowsy rather than DriveAlert’s separate EAR-, MAR-, and head-
pose-based events, DriveAlert’s mapping of a new distinct confirmed wa rning event to a newly 
occurring qualifying episode is an adaptation rather than a direct replication of their detection 
algorithm. Similarly, DriveAlert interprets continued satisfaction of a selected sign’s confirmed 
condition at a stage boundary as evid ence of persistent qualifying warning activity rather than 
claiming that the Driver has been continuously and medically confirmed as drowsy. The suitability 
of this mapping and the 60-second evaluation interval will therefore be examined during controlled 
testing using the actual DriveAlert implementation. 
For example, if a Driver first produces a confirmed prolonged-eye-closure event while no 
stage is active, DriveAlert immediately activates Stage 1. If the eye closure ends and the Driver 
later produces a distinct confirmed yawning event while Stage 1 remai ns active, the new event 
immediately progresses the system to Stage 2 and begins a new Stage 2 evaluation period. If a 
subsequent distinct head -nodding event occurs while Stage 2 is active, the system immediately 
progresses to Stage 3. In contrast, when additional signs become confirmed while an existing alert 
episode remains active under the episode-continuity rule, their signs are merged into that episode 
and do not independently advance the Warning Stage.  Likewise, during uninterrupted valid

26 
 
observation, keeping the eyes continuously closed after one prolonged -eye-closure confirmation 
does not repeatedly create new distinct alert episodes. Current -stage warning reminders may still 
be requested, while continued qualifying activity is separately evaluated at the applicable warning-
stage boundary. 
Warning Stage 1 will activate the Driver’s selected predefined warning sound through the 
IoT device. This represents the initial Driver-directed intervention following a confirmed warning 
event. Auditory warnings are widely represented in the Driver-state-monitoring literature reviewed 
by Ayas et al. (2024), while Chandana and Sangeetha (2023) similarly used a sound warning at the 
first level of their three-level system. 
Warning Stage 2 will retain the Driver’s selected predefined warning sound without adding 
a spoken advisory. It serves as an intermediate warning state when qualifying warning activity 
recurs during Stage 1 or remains persistently active at the Stage 1 eva luation boundary. Although 
Stages 1 and 2 use the same audio output, they represent different positions within the warning -
stage transition process. Ayas et al. (2024) support the broader use of staged interventions, while 
Chandana and Sangeetha (2023) pro vide precedent for introducing human -voice warnings after 
initial sound alerts. DriveAlert adapts these principles by reserving the spoken rest advisory for 
Warning Stage 3, where it is intended to distinguish the maximum intervention stage from the 
preceding sound-only warnings. The placement of speech at Stage 3 is a DriveAlert design decision 
rather than an arrangement directly prescribed by these sources. 
Chandana and Sangeetha (2023) provide a more direct precedent for reserving external 
communication for a final intervention level. Their three -level system initially provided a sound 
warning, progressed to a human -voice warning following repeated warning a ctivity, and used its 
third level as an alert-notification stage in which information including GPS data was transmitted 
to the vehicle owner or another concerned person. Their implementation therefore demonstrates an 
intervention structure progressing fro m an initial Driver -directed warning, to a stronger Driver -
directed warning, and finally to external awareness. 
Multi-feature Driver -monitoring approaches can reduce dependence on a single facial 
indicator when visual information is partially obstructed. Jia et al. (2021, 2022) demonstrated that 
monitoring could continue using the remaining observable facial features when the eyes or mouth 
were affected by sunglasses or face masks. DriveAlert applies this principle to supported mask and 
sunglasses detection and to facial measurements reported as unavailable by its processing pipeline. 
It does not claim to recognize every possible obstruction, such as all hands, phones, hair, scarves, 
or other objects. When one of the three monitored signs becomes unavailable while two remain 
reliable, DriveAlert continues in a degraded monitoring state and informs the Driver which

27 
 
capability is unavailable. If any two signs become unavailable, DriveAlert pauses drowsiness-sign 
monitoring rather than relying on a single behavioral indicator and instructs the Driver to restore 
sufficient facial visibility before monitoring resumes. 
Awasekar et al. (2018) provide additional precedent for placing external communication at 
a highest warning stage. Their Driver Fatigue Detection and Alert System used three fatigue stages 
based on its own eye-closure and yawning conditions. At Stage 3, the system combined its highest 
local intervention with communication to predefined contacts through an Android smartphone. 
DriveAlert does not adopt the fatigue -stage classifications used by Awasekar et al. because 
DriveAlert’s Warning Stages represent levels of system intervention rather than physiological or 
medical levels of Driver drowsiness. Their work nevertheless provides additional precedent for 
associating external communication with a final or highest intervention stage. 
Fitzharris et al. (2017) further demonstrated the value of supplementing Driver -directed 
warnings with external awareness in an operational Driver -monitoring environment. Their study 
examined a camera -based Driver -monitoring system that generated in -cab wa rnings and was 
subsequently combined with external monitoring and management feedback when fatigue events 
were identified. The external feedback condition produced a larger reduction in fatigue -event 
occurrence than the in -cab-warning condition alone under  the study conditions. Although 
DriveAlert’s Trusted Contact function differs from fleet -management intervention, the study 
supports the broader principle that external awareness can supplement immediate Driver -directed 
warnings when monitored warning activity persists. 
Warning Stage 3 will combine the Driver’s selected predefined warning sound with a fixed 
prerecorded spoken advisory recommending that the Driver stop in a safe place and take a rest. It 
will also introduce Trusted Contact synchronization eligibility. When DriveAlert progresses from 
Stage 2 to Stage 3, one Stage 3 transition record becomes eligible for synchronization with the 
Driver’s approved Trusted Contact, subject to internet availability. The introduction of speech 
following earlier sound warnings ada pts the progression described by Chandana and Sangeetha 
(2023), although DriveAlert places speech at Stage 3 rather than at their second intervention level. 
The exact advisory wording and its placement at Stage 3 are DriveAlert design decisions. Stage 3 
represents the maximum system intervention level following recurrent or persistent qualifying 
warning activity; it does not establish a medically severe level of Driver drowsiness. 
The three Warning Stages must therefore be interpreted as levels of system intervention 
rather than measurements of drowsiness severity. Warning Stage 1 represents the initial Driver -
directed intervention following the first distinct confirmed warning even t. Warning Stage 2 
represents an intermediate warning state that retains the selected warning sound when another

28 
 
distinct qualifying episode occurs while Stage 1 remains active or when qualifying warning activity 
persists through the Stage 1 evaluation boundary.  Warning Stage 3 represents the maximum 
intervention level when qualifying activity again recurs during Stage 2 or persists through the Stage 
2 evaluation boundary. DriveAlert does not infer that a Driver at Stage 3 has reached a medically 
established seve rity of drowsiness or is physiologically drowsier simply because the highest 
Warning Stage has been reached. 
Continued qualifying warning activity while Stage 3 remains active also requires an external -
awareness rule that does not generate a separate Trusted Contact synchronization record for every 
confirmed event. Schwarz et al. (2015) retained Stage 3 as the ma ximum mitigation stage and 
allowed the Stage 3 warning to be reissued when drowsiness persisted or recurred. Gaspar et al. 
(2017) similarly retained Stage 3 as the maximum countermeasure state and retriggered the Stage 
3 intervention when continued drowsin ess required another escalation. DriveAlert adapts this 
repeated maximum-stage principle to its Trusted Contact synchronization management.  
When DriveAlert initially enters Stage 3, one Stage 3 transition record becomes eligible 
for Trusted Contact synchronization. Individual distinct confirmed warning events occurring during 
the subsequent 60 -second Stage 3 evaluation period continue to be st ored in the Driver’s alert 
history and may reactivate the Stage 3 Driver-directed warning, but they do not each independently 
create a Trusted Contact synchronization record. Instead, they indicate that recurrent qualifying 
warning activity occurred during the active Stage 3 period. 
When the 60 -second Stage 3 period expires, DriveAlert evaluates both recurrent and persistent 
qualifying activity. If at least one additional distinct confirmed warning event occurred during the 
completed Stage 3 period, or if a qualifying behavior remains  persistently active at the Stage 3 
boundary, DriveAlert remains at Stage 3, begins another 60-second Stage 3 evaluation period, and 
creates one Stage 3 persistence update that becomes eligible for Trusted Contact synchronization. 
If neither condition is present, DriveAlert de-escalates to Stage 2 and no Stage 3 persistence update 
is created for that completed period. 
If qualifying warning activity continues across several consecutive Stage 3 periods, at most 
one persistence update becomes eligible for synchronization for each completed Stage 3 period in 
which recurrent or persistent qualifying warning activity is established. Individual warning events 
remain available in the Driver’s detailed alert history but do not independently produce external 
synchronization records. This separates detailed event recording from the frequency of Trusted 
Contact updates. 
The exact rule of generating one Trusted Contact persistence update per completed 
qualifying Stage 3 period is not a notification frequency directly prescribed by Schwarz et al.

29 
 
(2015), Gaspar et al. (2017), Chandana and Sangeetha (2023), Fitzharris et al. (2017), or the other 
reviewed studies. Schwarz et al. directly support maintaining Stage 3 as the maximum intervention 
level and reissuing its warning when drowsiness persists o r recurs, while Gaspar et al. directly 
support repeated Stage 3 intervention following continued drowsiness at a 60 -second 
countermeasure boundary. Chandana and Sangeetha provide precedent for external communication 
at the final intervention level, and Fitzharris et al. support supplementing Driver-directed warnings 
with external monitoring or feedback. DriveAlert combines these principles by aligning Trusted 
Contact persistence updates with its Stage 3 evaluation boundaries. The resulting persistence -
update rule is therefore a literature -informed DriveAlert information-management adaptation and 
will be evaluated during controlled testing for usefulness, unnecessary repetition, and 
synchronization behavior.  
For example, several distinct confirmed warning events occurring during one Stage 3 
evaluation period do not generate an equal number of Trusted Contact synchronization records. The 
events remain individually available in the Driver’s alert history, subject to the existing overlap and 
deduplication rules, while the completed Stage 3 period may produce one persistence update 
indicating that qualifying warning activity continued. This separates detailed event storage from 
external-awareness frequency. 
Trusted Contact synchronization remains subject to Driver approval and internet availability. Only 
eligible records from periods beginning on or after approval of the Driver –Trusted Contact 
relationship may be shared. Approval does not release the Driver’s earlier complete alert history, 
and continued access depends on the relationship remaining ap proved. If internet connectivity is 
unavailable when a Stage 3 transition or persistence update becomes synchronization-eligible, the 
corresponding record is retained in the synchronization queue until connectivity becomes available. 
Kashyap et al. (2025) demonstrated the use of Firebase and a web dashboard for remote review of 
Driver-status information, while Kumar et al. (2022) used SMS or email to provide drowsiness -
related information to authorized persons or family members. These studies support the broader 
technical feasibility of makin g selected Driver information available to an authorized external 
person. DriveAlert limits this feature to secondary awareness and record review and does not 
operate as an emergency-response service, guarantee immediate assistance, determine whether the 
Driver is fit to continue driving, or permit the Trusted Contact to control the Driver’s monitoring 
session. 
The Driver’s drowsiness-alert history and basic Drowsiness Insights feature are supported 
by literature on recorded-event visualization and dashboard-based review. Murphy et al. (2021) and 
Moens et al. (2021) demonstrated that dashboards can support review  of recorded safety -related

30 
 
events and trends. DriveAlert therefore allows Drivers to review confirmed warning events and 
basic descriptive summaries of stored records. These records and summaries are not intended as 
medical analysis, accident prediction, confirmation of drowsiness, or determination of the Driver’s 
fitness to continue driving. 
Overall, the reviewed literature supports the principal components of DriveAlert while 
showing that its three selected visible signs require different confirmation procedures. EAR, MAR, 
and head-pose measurements provide a basis for examining prolonged eye  closure, yawning, and 
head nodding, while Driver calibration addresses individual differences in facial measurements and 
neutral head orientation. Temporal evidence supports sustained confirmation of prolonged eye 
closure and yawning, while temporal persi stence provides a stronger basis for interpreting 
ambiguous downward head movement. Driver -monitoring literature further supports progressive 
multistage warning intervention. Schwarz et al. (2015) provide the primary basis for DriveAlert’s 
three-stage tran sition mechanics by describing incremental escalation when another drowsy 
episode occurs before the current mitigation abates or when drowsiness persists for 60 seconds, 
together with incremental abatement and Stage 3 as the maximum intervention level. Gaspar et al. 
(2017) later experimentally evaluated a related three -stage architecture using 60 -second 
countermeasure states and found that staged warnings reduced drowsy lane departures relative to 
single-stage warnings under the study conditions. Chandana and Sangeetha (2023) provide 
precedent for introducing human -voice warnings after initial sound alerts and external 
communication at a final intervention level. DriveAlert adapts these principles by retaining the 
selected warning sound during Stag es 1 and 2 and introducing both a spoken rest advisory and 
Trusted Contact synchronization eligibility at Stage 3. Fitzharris et al. (2017) provide evidence that 
external awareness or feedback can supplement immediate Driver -directed warnings. DriveAlert 
adapts these principles to distinct confirmed computer -vision warning events and controlled 
Trusted Contact synchronization while treating its Warning Stages as levels of system intervention 
rather than medical levels of drowsiness. Mobile-processing and IoT literature further supports 
DriveAlert’s local Android processing and local wireless communication, while its performance 
under different lighting conditions will be evaluated using the final camera configuration. 
 
Related Studies 
Deployed driver-drowsiness, fatigue, and alertness systems use mobile computer vision, 
wearable sensors, driver -condition assessment, and physical warning devices to help users 
recognize reduced alertness. Some systems monitor visible indicators such as eye closure and head 
movement, while others estimate fatigue using personal information, trip conditions, and reaction-

31 
 
time testing. These systems demonstrate that mobile, wearable, and embedded technologies can 
provide immediate warnings, although they differ in detection methods, hardware requirements, 
offline capability, record management, and user support. 
Drowsy Driving Alert is a deployed mobile application that uses artificial intelligence and 
the smartphone’s front camera to monitor the driver’s face and eyes. The application distinguishes 
normal blinking from extended eye closure and provides audio and visual alerts when drowsiness 
is detected. It can operate alongside Google Maps and Apple Maps, while facial processing is 
performed locally on the smartphone. However, the phone must be positioned where the camera 
can clearly view the driver. Lighting, ca mera obstruction, device performance, and background -
operation restrictions may also delay or interrupt warnings. 
WingDriver is a smartphone-based driver-monitoring system that uses computer vision and 
artificial intelligence to detect drowsiness, fatigue, distraction, and inattention. It provides 
immediate audible or visual warnings to help the driver regain attention. The provider also offers 
related business solut ions for fleets, ride -sharing services, insurers, and vehicle manufacturers. 
However, monitoring depends on the smartphone camera maintaining a usable view of the driver 
and on the mobile device having sufficient processing capability. Broader business deployment also 
requires coordination with the provider. 
Fatigue Alert – Stay Awake is a deployed application that uses supported AirPods or Beats 
headphones to monitor the user’s head posture. When downward head movement indicates possible 
drowsiness, the application provides warnings through sound, vibration, system notifications, or 
Apple Watch haptic feedback. It can continue operating in the background or while the device 
screen is locked. However, the system requires compatible Apple devices and supported 
headphones and focuses mainly on head-posture monitoring rather than facial indicators. It is also 
presented as a general stay-awake application rather than a system exclusively intended for driving. 
Anti Sleep Pilot is a dashboard -mounted device and mobile application that continuously 
calculates a driver’s fatigue level. Its calculation considers the driver’s personal risk profile, fatigue 
condition before the trip, and driving information registered  through built -in sensors. It also 
administers periodic reaction -time tests and provides audible and visual recommendations when 
the driver should take a break. However, the system requires initial profile configuration and 
periodic interaction from the dr iver. Its documentation also notes that low -speed traffic, GPS 
conditions, and some driving situations may affect trip-state interpretation or cause distraction. 
The alertme Drowsy Driver Device is a commercially deployed wearable warning device 
developed by resqme, Inc. It is worn behind the ear and detects downward head nodding associated 
with possible dozing. When the user’s head tilts forward by approximately 1 5 to 20 degrees, the

32 
 
battery-powered device produces a 90 -decibel audible alarm. The device does not require a 
smartphone, mobile application, or internet connection. However, it must be worn correctly, detects 
only head-nodding movement, and provides only a direct audible warning. 
The reviewed systems demonstrate different approaches to driver -state monitoring and 
warning. Drowsy Driving Alert and WingDriver use smartphone cameras and artificial intelligence 
to monitor visible driver behaviors. Fatigue Alert – Stay Awake uses wearable motion information 
to monitor head posture. Anti Sleep Pilot estimates fatigue through driver profiles, sensor 
information, and reaction-time testing. Meanwhile, alertme uses a simple wearable mechanism to 
detect downward head movement and produce an immediate alarm. 
The systems collectively show the progress and remaining integration gaps in driver -
drowsiness and alertness monitoring. Smartphone -based applications provide accessible camera 
monitoring but depend on phone placement, facial visibility, and device perform ance. Wearable 
applications require compatible accessories, while fatigue -estimation systems require profile 
configuration and periodic driver interaction. Simple physical alarms can operate without internet 
access but generally monitor only one behavior and do not provide organized records. 
Overall, DriveAlert combines selected driver -monitoring and record -management 
functions in an external-camera and Android-based prototype. Its configuration includes an external 
IoT camera with an infrared-capable sensor, Android-based local processing, offline IoT-to-mobile 
communication, monitoring of prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding, and onboard 
speaker warning output. Confirmed warning events are stored locally for Driver review and 
descriptive summaries, while separate eligible Stage 3 transition records and persistence updates 
support approved Trusted Contact sharing. DriveAlert investigates whether these functions can 
operate together under controlled testing conditions.

Software Engineering Methodology 
The development process for “DriveAlert: An IoT -Based Driver Drowsiness Monitoring 
and Alert System Using Computer Vision” will be based on the Agile methodology due to its 
iterative and flexible approach, which supports continuous improvement and frequent  testing of 
system features. In the case of DriveAlert, where the system involves driver drowsiness monitoring, 
alert triggering, drowsiness alert history recording, basic drowsiness insights, and Trusted Contact 
synchronization, Agile supports a development cycle that allows the researchers to improve the 
system based on testing results and user feedback. Agile’s emphasis on collaboration, feedback, 
and incremental progress provides a structured yet adaptable roadmap for the development process, 
helping the researchers manage system changes and ensure that the system requirements are 
addressed systematically.

Its 22 entities support personalized calibration, warning history, approved Trusted Contact sharing, 
and simulated additional -driver subscriptions. FK labels identify logical references; only 
relationships explicitly declared as Room foreign keys are enforced by SQL. 
User stores account identity, contact details, role, status, registration date, and connection 
code. The role identifies a Driver, Trusted Contact, or both. ConnectionCode associates an account 
lookup code with its owner, display name, creation date, and active status. Users enter these codes 
to request connections or invite additional Drivers. 
DriverPreference stores warning -sound selection, volume, notification preferences, history 
retention, and update time. MonitoringLogPreference separately stores the Driver’s retention 
setting for completed diagnostic logs. 
DriverCalibration stores personalized EAR, MAR, and head -pitch thresholds, calibration 
measurements, detector schema version, date, and active status. A Driver may retain multiple 
calibration records. MonitoringSession references the calibration used, preserving the relationship 
between each session and its detection thresholds. 
Device identifies a registered camera by its canonical Bluetooth identifier and claim marker. 
DeviceOwnership assigns one primary Driver to each device and stores its display name and 
registration metadata. ProvisionedDevice separately stores each Driver’s saved camera connection, 
including hostname, network address, stream settings, last connection time, and active status. Its 
composite key combines driverUserId and deviceId. MonitoringSession records the Driver, device, 
calibration, timing, status, and highest Warning Stage. 
TrustedContactConnection records the Driver, Trusted Contact, requester, target 
connection code, status, and request, approval, decline, and revocation times. Drivers and Trusted 
Contacts may have multiple approved connections. This relationship permits future eligible Stage 
3 sharing and is separate from additional-driver device access. 
Alert records confirmed warning events, including detection time, Warning Stage, onboard 
alarm status, and alarm-trigger time. AlertSign associates each event with prolonged eye closure, 
yawning, or head nodding. Warning Stages describe increasing system i ntervention rather than 
medical drowsiness severity. 
StageSyncRecord stores local Stage 3 transition and persistence records, including session 
references, warning -period boundaries, event counts, sharing eligibility, and synchronization 
metadata. StageSyncRecordSign identifies the detected signs. Eligible r ecords are published as

111 
 
SharedStage3Record documents in Cloud Firestore for approved Trusted Contacts. These records 
provide historical awareness rather than live camera monitoring. 
MonitoringLog and MonitoringLogEvent store diagnostic sessions and their timeline 
entries, including timing, measured values, thresholds, signs, durations, calibration references, 
Warning Stages, and alarm -response results. DeviceAccessGrant caches server -verified account 
access locally in Room, while DeviceIdentityMapping resolves older local identifiers to canonical 
device identifiers. 
DeviceDriverAccess stores invitations and additional-driver memberships, including their 
status, activation reference, and acceptance or ending times. DeviceSubscriptionEvent records 
simulated activations; no real payment is collected. DeviceCredential sto res account -specific 
authorization credentials. An invited Driver accepts and completes setup online, after which cached 
access and credentials permit offline device use. Each Driver retains separate calibration and alert 
history. Together, these records s upport one included primary Driver per device and controlled 
access for additional Drivers.

Implementation/Deployment Phase 
This section covers the installation and configuration of DriveAlert for use by Drivers and 
Trusted Contacts. It includes installing the Android application, uploading the ESP32 -CAM 
firmware, preparing the camera and onboard warning components, configuring  Firebase services, 
and deploying the Trusted Contact web portal through Firebase Hosting. Device registration and 
initial authorization require an internet connection. Once setup is complete, authorized Drivers can 
monitor offline while maintaining separate calibration and alert histories. This phase also includes 
user orientation and verification of camera connectivity, calibration, monitoring, onboard warnings, 
and eligible Stage 3 record sharing before deployment. 
Deployment Diagram 
This section illustrates how DriveAlert’s components are distributed across devices and 
network environments. It shows the connections among the ESP32 -CAM and its warning 
components, the Android application that processes camera frames and stores local rec ords, 
Firebase services, and the Trusted Contact web portal. It also distinguishes local communication 
used for setup, monitoring, and warnings from internet connections used for account management, 
device authorization, and shared-record synchronization.

The deployment diagram presents DriveAlert’s architecture, showing the connections

frames and transmit them to the Driver’s phone through a local Wi -Fi HTTP/MJPEG connection.

1. Introduction 
DriveAlert is an IoT-based Driver drowsiness monitoring and alert system using computer 
vision. Its Android application processes frames from an ESP32-CAM to recognize prolonged eye 
closure, yawning, and head nodding using the Driver's calibration. Confirm ed events produce 
warning stages and are saved in the Driver's alert history. Approved Trusted Contacts can review 
eligible Stage 3 records through the mobile application or web portal. 
The Android application uses Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, and Room for local records. 
Firebase supports accounts, connections, device access, and shared records, while the React and 
TypeScript web portal serves Trusted Contacts. After initial online setup, aut horized Drivers can 
monitor offline. Eligible shared records synchronize when internet access becomes available.

2.1 System Configuration 
The mobile application runs on Android 8.0 or higher. Drivers use Wi -Fi for camera 
streaming and warning commands, and Bluetooth Low Energy for device setup and authorization. 
Monitoring requires a connected camera, confirmed alignment, and an active Drive r calibration. 
The phone performs vision processing and stores local records. 
Trusted Contacts can also open https://drivealert.web.app in a web browser. Internet access 
is required for registration, email verification, connection requests, device invitations, and loading 
cloud records. Saved local history can be reviewed without reconnecting the camera. Android and 
browser history preferences are managed separately.

Driver connections. 
Driver: Uses the Android application to complete setup, start and stop monitoring, review 
personal alerts and insights, manage warning preferences, and approve or remove Trusted Contacts. 
Trusted Contact: Uses the Android application or web portal to manage Driver 
connections and review approved shared historical records. This view does not provide live camera 
video, vehicle location, or complete Driver history.

CONCLUSION 
Based on the data gathered, the proponents concluded that DriveAlert: An IoT -Based 
Driver Drowsiness Monitoring and Alert System Using Computer Vision is a beneficial innovation 
for supporting driver awareness and monitoring visible signs associated with d rowsiness. Drivers 
may experience prolonged eye closure, yawning, and head nodding without immediately 
recognizing the need to stop and rest. Relying on personal awareness alone may allow these signs 
to go unnoticed, while the absence of organized alert re cords limits opportunities for reviewing 
recurring events and keeping Trusted Contacts informed. These concerns highlight the need for an 
integrated system that can assist Drivers through monitoring, warning alerts, and record sharing. 
With DriveAlert, Dri vers are provided with a platform that uses an IoT camera and an Android 
application to monitor selected visible signs through computer vision and personalized calibration. 
Through local Wi-Fi communication, the application processes camera frames without requiring 
internet access during monitoring after initial setup and sends warning commands to an onboard 
speaker. Its dashboard allows Drivers to review alert history and basic insights, while eligible Stage 
3 records are synchronized with approved Trusted Contacts through the mobile application or web 
portal when internet connectivity becomes available. Ultimately, DriveAlert offers a practical 
approach to combining local monitoring, audible warnings, and approved record sharing, helping 
Drivers recognize warning events and enabling Trusted Contacts to remain informed while 
supporting safer driving decisions.
